Official Week 3 Objectives

1. Explain the body's fuel composition; define basal metabolic rate (BMR), identify factors affecting it, and calculate daily energy expenditure.
2. Calculate the caloric content of a diet and estimate whether it would support weight gain or weight loss.
3. Define body mass index (BMI) and describe its calculation and the lecture's categorization framework, including waist-circumference context.
Assigned ScholarRx
Regulation of Appetite (official LO sheet notes only some lecture concepts are covered) • Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome

Slides 2–4: Energy Homeostasis & Food as Fuel

Slide 2. Energy homeostasis is framed as Energy In versus Energy Out: persistent excess favors growth/obesity; persistent deficit favors slimming/starvation.
Slide 3. The core equation is Energy In = Energy Out, with Food balanced against exertion plus basal metabolic requirements. BMR is defined as minimum resting energy expenditure required to sustain life.
Slide 4. The lecture assigns 4 kcal/g to carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g to fat, and 4 kcal/g to protein, while noting protein must be deaminated before its carbon can be used as fuel.
Calculation anchor
Carbohydrate 4 kcal/g • Protein 4 kcal/g • Fat 9 kcal/g.
2029 AI Notes enrichment: the older handout also lists ethanol at 7 kcal/g. That value is not shown on the current lecture slide, so it stays enrichment rather than a core deck fact.

Slides 5–7: TDEE, Thermic Effect & BMR

Slide 5. Daily energy use is broken into sleeping/resting metabolism, arousal, thermic effect of food, spontaneous activity (NEAT), and unrestricted/exercise activity (EAT).
Slide 6. Thermic effect of food is the postprandial rise in metabolic rate. The slide emphasizes protein as producing the largest thermic response, with carbohydrate intermediate and lipid lower.
Slide 7. BMR determinants listed in the deck include body size, age, lean mass, sex, temperature, diet, genetics, neural output, enzyme isoforms, and circulating hormones—especially thyroid hormone.
BMR distinction
Raw BMR = calories/day. Normalized BMR = calories/kg/day.
2029 AI Notes enrichment: the handout supplies approximate TEF ranges (protein highest; carbohydrate intermediate; lipid lowest) and explicitly links excess thyroid hormone with a higher BMR and low thyroid hormone with a lower BMR. The current deck itself simply lists thyroid hormone as a major determinant.

Slide 8: Tissue-Specific Fuel Use

Slide 8. The slide contrasts fuel preferences in brain, muscle, liver, adipose, and heart.
TissueLecture emphasis
BrainRequires glucose; can use ketones in severe deprivation. Fatty acids/amino acids do not supply it sufficiently across the BBB.
MuscleLarge glycogen store for its own use; glucose for short high activity, fatty acids dominate at rest.
LiverStores glucose for other organs, performs gluconeogenesis, processes lipids into lipoproteins, and produces fuels for other tissues.
AdiposeMajor fat reserve; low glucose favors fat release.
HeartVery high fuel demand; uses fatty acids, lactate, and ketones and stores little fuel.

Slides 9–17: Positive Energy Balance, BMI & Leptin

Slide 9. The lecture contrasts dietary/activity factors that favor obesity with factors that oppose it and highlights thyroid hormone and sympathetic output as hormonal influences.
Slide 10. BMI is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. The slide uses its own lecture-specific category labels.
Use the deck's terminology when studying this lecture. The slide labels <18.5 “Thin,” 18.5–24.9 “Height Weight Proportional,” 25–29.9 “Grade I Overweight,” 30–39.9 “Grade II Overweight (Obese),” and >40 “Grade III Overweight (Morbidly Obese).” This companion preserves that source terminology rather than silently replacing it with an outside classification.
Slide 12. A lifetime-energy example shows how a very small chronic caloric mismatch can accumulate into a large change in body mass, underscoring tight physiologic control of energy balance.
Slide 13. The deck presents lifestyle excess/inactivity as the dominant explanation for most excess weight while also noting genetic contributions to obesity, naming leptin, POMC, and MC4R among candidate genes.
Slide 14. Leptin is presented as the product of the ob gene and as a protein signal linked to adipose tissue and nutrient status.
Slide 15. The lecture's leptin physiology model: adipose-derived leptin acts on the hypothalamus to increase anorexic signals and decrease orexic signals, reducing food intake as energy stores fall.
Slide 16. Leptin and sympathetic signaling are presented as a feedback loop: leptin stimulates SNS activity, while sympathetic stimulation of adipocytes reduces leptin production/expression.
Slide 17. Genetic leptin loss is described as extremely rare, while common obesity is associated with high circulating leptin and leptin resistance; therefore routine leptin therapy is ineffective in most obesity.
Leptin pattern
Rare deficiency = low leptin and can respond dramatically to replacement. Common obesity = hyperleptinemia + leptin resistance.

Slides 18–19: Weight Loss & Starvation

Slide 18. The deck emphasizes that calories lost drive weight loss and discusses why changing macronutrient composition does not bypass overall energy balance.
Slide 19. Energy deprivation progresses from short-term liver glycogen use and gluconeogenesis, to increased ketone production and protein sparing, and finally to accelerated protein breakdown once fat stores are depleted. Loss of immune function and infection are emphasized late in starvation.

Prolonged fasting

Use liver glycogen first, then increase gluconeogenesis; muscle shifts toward more fat use.

Extended deprivation

Ketone production rises; brain gains an alternate fuel; nonessential protein can support gluconeogenesis and renal gluconeogenesis increases.

Starvation

Once fat is depleted, protein breakdown accelerates and essential cellular/tissue function is lost.

Late consequence

Loss of immune function raises susceptibility to infection, described in the deck as the most common cause of death due to starvation.

Last 60 Seconds

Energy in vs energy out • 4/4/9 kcal per g for carb/protein/fat • TDEE = resting + TEF + NEAT + exercise activity • BMR rises with size/lean mass/youth/temperature and is strongly influenced by thyroid status • know tissue fuel preferences • BMI = kg/m² • common obesity = high leptin + resistance • starvation shifts glycogen → gluconeogenesis/fat → ketones → terminal protein loss.
